config.title: Build typed error hierarchy classes

intro.title: Build typed error hierarchy classes
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a hierarchy of custom error classes using TypeScript. You'll learn how to create a base error class and extend it to define more specific error types, like a 'ValidationError' or 'NetworkError'. The core concept is using class inheritance to structure errors in a way that makes them easier to catch and handle in your code. You'll work with TypeScript features such as classes, the 'extends' keyword, and custom constructors. By the end, you'll have a reusable error system that improves the reliability and clarity of your applications.
intro.usecase: In real-world applications, typed error hierarchies are essential for handling different failure scenarios in a structured way. For example, in an e-commerce dashboard, you might have specific error classes for payment failures (PaymentError), inventory issues (InventoryError), and shipping lessons (ShippingError), each with their own properties and recovery logic. This pattern allows developers to catch and handle errors precisely in different UI components like checkout forms, order management panels, or inventory modals. By creating a hierarchy of typed errors, you ensure consistent error handling across your application while providing clear debugging information and user-friendly error messages.

objectives: Construct a base error class with typed properties in TypeScript
Implement custom error classes that extend the base error hierarchy
Apply inheritance principles to create specialized error types
Configure error instances with structured metadata and messages
Manipulate error objects to include contextual information
Integrate typed error classes into a sample error handling flow
Initialize error hierarchies with proper constructors and super calls

steps.title: Create a base Error class with typed properties
steps.instruction: Create a base Error class called AppError that extends the native Error class and adds typed properties like statusCode and timestamp.
steps.hint: Start by declaring a class named AppError that extends Error, then add typed properties in the constructor.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a custom AppError class that extends Error with typed statusCode and timestamp properties.
successCriteria: The AppError class extends Error and includes typed statusCode and timestamp properties in its constructor.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure AppError extends Error and includes both statusCode and timestamp as typed properties.
steps.feedbackWrong: The AppError class should extend Error and include typed statusCode and timestamp properties. Try again.

steps.title: Add constructor with typed parameters to AppError
steps.instruction: Inside your AppError class, add a constructor that accepts two typed parameters: message (string) and statusCode (number). In the constructor body, assign these parameters to the class properties and set timestamp to the current date using new Date().
steps.hint: Remember to use the 'this' keyword to assign the parameters to the class properties. For timestamp, you can use new Date() to get the current date.
steps.expectedOutcome: The AppError class now has a constructor that properly initializes all properties with the correct types.
successCriteria: AppError has a constructor with typed message (string) and statusCode (number) parameters that assigns values to class properties and sets timestamp to new Date()
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your constructor has both message and statusCode parameters with correct types, and sets timestamp to new Date().
steps.feedbackWrong: The constructor doesn't match the requirements. It needs to accept message (string) and statusCode (number) parameters and set timestamp to the current date.

steps.title: Create a NotFoundError class extending AppError
steps.instruction: Create a new class named NotFoundError that extends the AppError class. Inside the class, add a constructor that calls super() with a message parameter and sets a default statusCode of 404.
steps.hint: Use the 'extends' keyword to inherit from AppError. In the constructor, call super(message) and set this.statusCode = 404.
steps.expectedOutcome: A NotFoundError class is created that inherits from AppError and automatically sets statusCode to 404.
successCriteria: NotFoundError class extends AppError, has a constructor that calls super(message) and sets this.statusCode = 404.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure NotFoundError extends AppError and sets statusCode to 404 in the constructor.
steps.feedbackWrong: The NotFoundError class is missing or doesn't properly extend AppError with the required constructor.

steps.title: Add custom constructor to NotFoundError
steps.instruction: Inside the NotFoundError class, add a constructor that accepts a single 'message' parameter and calls super() with that message and the status code 404.
steps.hint: The constructor should take a string parameter for the message and pass it along with the fixed status code 404 to the parent AppError constructor.
steps.expectedOutcome: The NotFoundError class will have a constructor that automatically sets the status code to 404 when instantiated.
successCriteria: NotFoundError has a constructor that takes a message parameter and calls super(message, 404).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure your constructor accepts a message parameter and passes it along with 404 to super().
steps.feedbackWrong: That's not quite right. The constructor should take a message parameter and call super(message, 404).

steps.title: Create a ValidationError class extending AppError
steps.instruction: Create a new class named ValidationError that extends AppError. Add a fieldErrors property with the type Record<string, string> to this class.
steps.hint: Remember to use the 'extends' keyword to inherit from AppError, and declare the fieldErrors property with its type before the constructor.
steps.expectedOutcome: A ValidationError class is created that extends AppError and includes a fieldErrors property with the correct type.
successCriteria: The ValidationError class extends AppError and has a fieldErrors property of type Record<string, string>.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure ValidationError extends AppError and includes the fieldErrors property with the correct type.
steps.feedbackWrong: The ValidationError class is missing or doesn't properly extend AppError with the required fieldErrors property.

steps.title: Implement ValidationError constructor with fieldErrors
steps.instruction: Add a constructor to the ValidationError class that accepts three parameters: message (string), fieldErrors (object with string keys and string array values), and an optional statusCode (number, default 400).
steps.hint: Remember to call super() with the required parameters and assign the fieldErrors property.
steps.expectedOutcome: The ValidationError class will have a properly typed constructor that handles complex error data with fieldErrors.
successCriteria: ValidationError constructor accepts message (string), fieldErrors (Record<string, string[]>), and optional statusCode (number, default 400), calls super(), and assigns fieldErrors.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure your constructor has all three parameters with correct types and calls super() properly.
steps.feedbackWrong: The constructor doesn't match the required signature. Check the parameter types and default value for statusCode.

steps.title: Create a function to simulate throwing NotFoundError
steps.instruction: Create a function named findUser that takes a userId parameter of type string and throws a NotFoundError when the userId is 'invalid'.
steps.hint: Define the function with the findUser name, include a parameter with type annotation, and use a conditional to throw the error.
steps.expectedOutcome: A findUser function is defined that conditionally throws a NotFoundError.
successCriteria: The findUser function exists, accepts a string userId parameter, and throws a NotFoundError when userId is 'invalid'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your function includes the userId parameter with type string and throws the NotFoundError when the condition is met.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function is missing or doesn't match the requirements. Ensure you define findUser with the correct signature and throwing logic.

steps.title: Create a function to simulate throwing ValidationError
steps.instruction: Create a function named 'validateUserInput' that throws a ValidationError with fieldErrors when the input is invalid. The function should take a 'username' string parameter and validate that it's not empty and at least 3 characters long.
steps.hint: Define a function that checks the username length and throws a ValidationError with appropriate fieldErrors if validation fails.
steps.expectedOutcome: A validateUserInput function is created that throws ValidationError with fieldErrors when username validation fails.
successCriteria: The validateUserInput function exists, takes a username parameter, validates it, and throws ValidationError with appropriate fieldErrors object.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created a function, but make sure it properly validates the username and throws ValidationError with a fieldErrors object.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function doesn't exist or doesn't properly throw ValidationError with fieldErrors. Review how to create functions that throw typed errors.

steps.title: Implement error handling with instanceof checks
steps.instruction: Create a function named handleError that takes an error parameter and uses instanceof checks to handle AppError, NotFoundError, and ValidationError with appropriate console.log responses.
steps.hint: Define a function that accepts an error parameter, then use if/else if statements with instanceof to check the error type and log different messages.
steps.expectedOutcome: A handleError function that demonstrates type-safe error handling using instanceof type narrowing.
successCriteria: The handleError function exists, accepts an error parameter, and uses instanceof checks for AppError, NotFoundError, and ValidationError with different console.log messages.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure your handleError function includes instanceof checks for all three error types (AppError, NotFoundError, ValidationError) with different console.log responses.
steps.feedbackWrong: The handleError function doesn't properly implement instanceof checks for the error hierarchy. Review how to use instanceof with custom classes and ensure you handle all three error types.

steps.title: Test the error hierarchy with example usage
steps.instruction: Create a function named demonstrateErrorHandling that calls findUser and validateUserInput with example arguments, catches errors using the existing handleError function, and logs appropriate messages to the console.
steps.hint: Call findUser with a non-existent ID (like 999) and validateUserInput with invalid data (like an empty string). Wrap each call in a try-catch block and pass caught errors to handleError.
steps.expectedOutcome: A function that tests the error hierarchy by triggering both NotFoundError and ValidationError scenarios, demonstrating type-safe error handling in action.
successCriteria: The demonstrateErrorHandling function exists, calls findUser and validateUserInput with appropriate arguments, uses try-catch blocks, and passes caught errors to handleError.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've started the demonstration function, but make sure it calls both findUser and validateUserInput with arguments that trigger errors, and uses try-catch with handleError.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function doesn't exist or doesn't properly demonstrate error handling. Create demonstrateErrorHandling that tests both error scenarios with try-catch blocks.
